paras: The lynching of Elijah Clark took place on July 23, 1900, when a mob took Clark, a young Black man accused of assaulting a 13-year-old girl, from the Madison County jail in Huntsville, Alabama, and hanged him. The mob, put at 1,000 to 2,000 men, used dynamite and a smoking fire to overcome Sheriff Fulgham, who was carried out unconscious. White papers told the story as a contest between a determined mob and a sheriff who would not give up his prisoner.

According to a Birmingham special, the alleged assault took place at Dallas, "a factory suburb of Huntsville," and the girl was Susie Priest, aged thirteen. The Huntsville wire named her Susan Priest and placed the attack on the Sunday before the lynching. The Keowee Courier of South Carolina gave her age as twelve, called her white, and said Clark was twenty. Two deputies caught Clark after an all-night search and jailed him.

A crowd formed at once, including 500 men from Dallas. Sheriff Fulgham promised a speedy trial and announced a special term of court under Judge Speak at 3 o'clock, but the crowd hooted him. Shots were fired, and two cotton-factory laborers, William Vining and Thomas Johnson, were carried off wounded, Vining dangerously. One wire version said Vining was shot "by the sheriff" as he rushed the steps, while the Keowee Courier said deputies fired on the crowd.

At noon dynamite exploded on the front steps of the jail, damaging the entrance. One wire said Governor Johnston ordered out militia that arrived too late; the Birmingham special said the troops lacked ammunition and were not called. Late in the day the mob battered down the doors and burned tar, feathers and oil on the corridor floor to smoke out the defenders.

The sheriff retreated with his prisoner to the third floor and held out until he lost consciousness, when the chief of police dragged him from the building. The mob broke open the cell and, according to the Keowee Courier and one wire, brought Clark before the girl, who identified him. He was then hanged from a tree at Dallas, near the place of the alleged assault, and his body was "riddled with bullets."

No report of an inquest, arrests or a trial appears in the coverage. A later Huntsville special reported that Dallas Mills residents, fearing Black residents would "get even," had distributed 300 Winchester rifles. It added a claim, "reported on reliable authority," that 300 Black men had met secretly in Shelta caverns.

Most white papers carried a short Huntsville wire under headlines such as "Vengeance of a Mob" and "Smoked the Sheriff Out." Versions of it ran in weeklies such as the Hope Pioneer, the Ely Miner and the Eagle River Review. Its subheadline in the Willmar Tribune read "Wreaked on a Brutal Negro," and it stated the assault as fact.

South Carolina weeklies added comment of their own. The Keowee Courier called the lynching "condign punishment" and Clark's body "a ghastly warning to living brutes such as he." The Manning Times, under "A Determined Mob," admired both the mob's "grave determination" and the sheriff's "dogged resistance," and called Clark "a negro rapist." A week later the Abbeville Press and Banner printed the fullest account, "Jail Stormed With Fire," which credited the sheriff with keeping the mob "at bay all day long."

The Black press gave the lynching little space. The Savannah Tribune printed the Dallas Mills dispatch without comment among other briefs. The Cleveland Gazette listed "Alabama, with its lynching" with North Carolina's red shirts and the New Orleans mob, and faulted the president for saying "not a word" against mob violence. The Indianapolis Freeman reprinted a Northern editorial that cited "the lynching at Huntsville, the other day" as proof that mob law was "the instant penalty" for an alleged outrage on a woman.

The mob numbered 1,000 according to the Keowee Courier and the Manning Times, and 2,000 according to the Birmingham special. The girl was thirteen in the wire and the Birmingham special but twelve in the Keowee Courier. The wire placed the seizure on Monday night; the more detailed Birmingham special described a siege ending late in the afternoon.
